title: Balanced and unbalanced forces: tug of war
subject: Physics

steps.title: Ropes
steps.instruction: Trace both ropes and the flags tied to their middles.

note.text: In tug of war, two teams pull a rope in opposite directions. The flag shows which way the rope moves.

steps.title: Balanced pulls
steps.instruction: Draw the two arrows for the top rope. They're the same length.

note.text: An arrow shows a force: it points in the force's direction, and a longer arrow means a stronger force. Equal and opposite forces are balanced.
note.remember: Balanced forces: no change in motion.

steps.title: Unbalanced pulls
steps.instruction: Draw the two arrows for the bottom rope. The left one is longer.

note.text: When one pull is stronger, the forces are unbalanced. Unbalanced forces change an object's motion.

steps.title: Motion
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow showing which way the bottom flag moves.

note.text: The rope moves toward the stronger pull. The bigger the difference between the forces, the faster its motion changes.

steps.title: Predict
steps.question: In the top rope, both teams pull equally hard. What happens to the flag?

options.feedback: Right. The forces are balanced, so the rope's motion doesn't change: it stays still.
That needs a stronger pull to the left. These pulls are equal.
That needs a stronger pull to the right. These pulls are equal.
Equal pulls don't move the rope. A rope only breaks if the forces are too big for it.

steps.title: Change it
steps.question: How could the right-hand team stop the flag from moving left?

options.text: Pull harder until both pulls are equal
options.feedback: Yes. Making the forces equal balances them, and the rope stops changing its motion.
Then only the left team pulls, and the flag moves left even faster.
A weaker pull makes the difference bigger, so the flag moves left faster.
Balancing the forces stops the change in motion.
